problem: Legged robots cannot easily collect large-scale navigation data, and human demonstrations captured from a different camera perspective and with different dynamics (and no robot action labels) cannot be directly used for imitation learning.
motivation: Humans are faster and safer to collect data from than legged robots, so learning from human demos would ease the data bottleneck. This needs perspective-invariant state features and robot-compatible action labels, and a planner that works in that feature space for zero-shot goal-image navigation.
key_idea: Learn perspective-invariant state features from temporally aligned multi-camera human videos with a cycle-loss feature disentanglement network, then train a UPN-style model-based imitation planner in that latent space using action labels from a learned inverse dynamics model or a GUI.
insight: Direct transfer across perspectives fails (UPN-PerspChange gets 7.88% vs 54.55% for the method on NavWorld), while the FDN nearly closes the gap to same-perspective UPN (58.00%), so disentangling state from perspective is what matters. The cycle-loss with a decoder is more stable than a triplet loss alone (NavWorld 4 steps: 54.55% vs 8.77%). Performance falls with start-goal distance and rises with more demonstrations.
method: Feature Disentanglement Network (FDN): a state encoder F and a perspective encoder P (CycleGAN encoder backbone, d=256 flattened features) plus a decoder R. All are trained on temporally aligned multi-perspective human images.

Cycle-loss: swap the state and perspective features of two images, so R(F(I_i^p), P(I_j^q)) must reconstruct I_i^q. This forces F to be perspective-invariant and P to be state-invariant, with no extra supervision.

Action labeling: an inverse dynamics model on FDN features of consecutive frames labels human demos with robot actions, trained on random robot rollouts (up to 30 steps or until collision). This is used in simulation. A manual GUI is used for real-robot data.

Model-based imitation (UPN-like): a latent forward model M predicts future features from the current feature and an action sequence. Gradient descent on the actions minimizes the Huber loss between the predicted final feature and the goal feature. M is trained so the optimized actions match the human expert actions, using a mask for variable horizon.

Policy execution: the policy replans the whole action sequence at every step and executes only the first action (MPC-style). Actions are 5 discrete high-level commands executed by a Raibert controller. The goal is an image from the human perspective.
Data augmentation: time-reversed replay of demos and added stay-in-place sequences. Real data uses 3 body-mounted GoPro cameras at different heights and angles.

setting.backbone: CycleGAN-style encoder/decoder FDN + latent forward model (trained from scratch, UPN-style planner)
setting.training_data: Simulation: 500 planner-generated human demos of 20 steps each, plus robot random-walk data for the inverse dynamics model. Real: 25 human demos of 20 steps each (about 10 min) from 3 cameras, with manual GUI action labels. Time-reversal augmentation is applied.
setting.observation: monocular RGB 128x128 from the robot camera; goal is an RGB image from the human perspective
setting.action_space: 5 discrete high-level actions (forward, backward, turn left, turn right, stay) executed by a Raibert leg controller; about 0.2 m per step, turn ~30° (NavWorld) or 90° (OfficeWorld)
setting.privileged: Temporally aligned multi-perspective human demonstrations for training; action labels via GUI or IDM; none at test time

numbers.extra: 500 human demos; the same-perspective UPN upper bound is 58.00%

numbers_note: Results are on custom PyBullet worlds and a small real-robot test, not standard benchmarks. The real-robot success rate is only given as 'around 60%'.
results: In simulation the method reaches 20-80% success depending on start-goal distance. At 4 steps in NavWorld it gets 54.55%, close to the same-perspective UPN upper bound of 58.00% and far above UPN-PerspChange at 7.88%. On the real Laikago it succeeds about 60% of the time on ~2 m goals.
limitations: Real-robot action labeling needs a manual GUI, because an inverse dynamics model fails on a legged robot (gait blur, noisy actions).
Success drops sharply with longer start-goal distance (about 22-27% at 10 steps), and the real-robot evaluation is tiny (9 trials, small room) with success judged visually.
It struggles with goals visually similar to the background, and the setup assumes kinematic motion and discrete coarse actions.
